title.en: Agentic payments: how an AI could shop and pay for you

en.title: Agentic payments: software that shops and pays for you
lines: Hello, and welcome to Oh, I Get It! Complex things, explained with everyday life.
Today's topic is agentic payments: software that shops and pays for you.
I know which shop is cheapest for detergent and soap. I also know where milk and cheese are the best quality.
But we're a bit lazy. Visiting two shops for two kinds of items is a hassle, so we end up compromising.
What if an AI agent did the checking, and even made the payment for us?
Here's how that could work.

en.heading: Step 1: Set up once
items: phone | Add your card | Like adding a card to your phone wallet
fingerprint | Bank checks it's you | Fingerprint or a code
card | Agent gets a stand-in | Not your real card
list | You set the rules | Milk and cheese: M&S / Limit: £25
lines: Step one: a one-time setup.
You register your card with the agent, a bit like adding a card to your phone wallet.
Your bank checks it's really you, with a fingerprint or a code.
The agent is then designed to hold a digital stand-in for your card, not the card itself.
Then you set the rules: milk and cheese must come from M&S, for quality, and no more than £25 in total.

en.heading: Step 2: Ask for quotes
items: list | Your shopping list | Detergent, soap, / milk, cheese
shop | Shop A | Sends a quote
shop | Shop B | Sends a quote
shop | M&S | Sends a quote
en.note: A request for quote is called an RFQ.
lines: Step two: ask.
Just like getting three quotes for a kitchen, the agent sends your shopping list to every supermarket in town.
In business, that's called a request for quote, or RFQ.
Detergent, soap, milk and cheese.

en.heading: Step 3: Compare the totals
items: lock | Your rule is locked in | Milk and cheese: M&S
scales | Compare the totals | Detergent and soap, / one total per shop
tick! | Lowest total wins | The rest of the basket / goes there
lines: Step three: compare.
The quotes come back, and the agent adds up the total for each shop.
It follows your rule: milk and cheese are locked to M&S.
The detergent and soap go to whichever shop gives the lowest total.

en.heading: A made-up example
items: shop | Shop A | Detergent £3.90 / Soap £3.50 / Total £7.40
shop! | Shop B | Detergent £4.10 / Soap £3.00 / Total £7.10 / Wins on the total
lock | M&S | Milk and cheese, / locked in
en.note: Example prices, made up for this video.
lines: In this made-up example, shop A charges £3.90 for detergent and £3.50 for soap, £7.40 in total.
Shop B charges £4.10 and £3.00, £7.10 in total.
Shop B isn't cheapest on everything, but it wins on the total.
Add the M&S milk and cheese, and the basket is complete.

en.heading: Step 4: Pay
items: agent | The agent pays | The stand-in, for just that amount and shop
shield | The shop checks | Is this a genuine agent?
network | Card network checks | Is the payment valid?
tick! | Your bank approves | Like any card payment
lines: Step four: pay.
For each shop, the agent uses the stand-in for just that purchase: that amount, that shop.
The shop checks two things. Is this a genuine agent? And does the card network confirm the payment is valid?
Your bank then approves it, like any card payment.

en.heading: Over your limit?
items: pound | Your limit | £25 in total
stop | The agent stops | The total is above the limit
alert | You get asked | Approve it, or say no
lines: If the total goes above the limit you set, the agent stops and asks you.
Same as a builder's quote coming in higher than agreed.

en.heading: Who is building this?
items: shield | Permission | Example: Google's AP2
id | Identity | Examples: Visa and Mastercard agent checks
card | Payment | Examples: Visa and Mastercard
lines: Visa, Mastercard, Google and others are building the parts for this: permission, identity and payment.
Treat this video as an example of what could be possible, not something you can do today.

en.heading: Who pays if it goes wrong?
items: question | The open question | Is an agent's payment / counted as authorised?
bank | Your bank | Refunds an unauthorised / payment first
scales | The FCA | Firms stay responsible
lines: One question isn't settled. If the agent orders the wrong thing, who pays?
The rules say that if a payment wasn't authorised, your bank refunds you first. It can then claim the money back from the payment firm at fault.
But is a payment your agent made authorised? That's the open question.
On 24 November the FCA said firms stay responsible.

en.heading: Until then
items: pound | Set a limit | Cap what it can spend
alert | Approve big buys | Ask for your OK
shield | Protect your card | Don't share card details with tools you don't understand
lines: Until then, set a spending limit, approve the big buys, and don't share your card details with a tool you don't understand.
This is education, not financial advice.
